title: 2  Preface
text:
Just matter of what was libido for Freud, this is my little contribution to a topic that I am very passionate about.
These notes are my attempt to truly understand how VAR models work, going into the details to see how the mechanisms behind them operate, with simple examples that make each step clear. Most of the material is based on lectures by Professor Roberto Golinelli, the Macroeconometric Forecasting (MFx) course by the IMF, Hamilton, J. D. (1994) and Stock, J. H., & Watson, M. W. (2001).
They may be useful if you already have a basic knowledge of time series analysis, and more specifically of AR models.

title: 3  VAR intro
text:
3.1 What is VAR?
At first sight, VARs (Vector AutoRegressive models) may seem a simple multivariate generalization of univariate AR models. After a closer inspection, however, they prove to be one of the central empirical instruments in contemporary macroeconomics, so much so that they have become one of the key empirical tools of modern applied macroeconomic analysis.

text:
3.4 How VAR is used in macroeconometrics?
VAR offers a coherent and credible framework for four distinct tasks: data description, forecasting, structural inference and policy analysis.
For forecasting and data description, a reduced-form VAR is sufficient: forecasting only requires the conditional mean of future values given the past, with no need to take a stance on the underlying structural relationships among the variables.
For structural inference and policy analysis, however, the reduced-form VAR is not enough, these tasks require an identified VAR10. In this context, the goal is to analyze the impact of structural shocks. This is done with impulse-response analysis11 and with forecast error variance decomposition12.
Two main ways to identify a VAR, and so to identify structural shocks’ effects:
Recursive ordering: impose a causal chain among variables (via Cholesky decomposition), assuming that the first variable in the VAR affects all the others within the period, while the second affects all except the first, and so on.
Structural approach: impose restrictions derived from economic theory on which variables affect which others within the same period, instead of relying on an arbitrary mechanical ordering.
More about both approaches later in Chapter 5.

title: 3  VAR intro
3  VAR intro
text:
Multivariate: VAR models several variables jointly, not just one. Each variable depends on its own lags and on the lags of all other variables in the system. (Univariate AR: only own past values. VAR: own past + others’ past.)↩︎
Joint dynamics: All variables move together and influence each other over time, not “multiple” series side by side.↩︎
Endogenous vs. exogenous: an endogenous variable is determined within the system, the model explains it, and it can be both cause and effect of the others. An exogenous variable is taken as given from outside the system, it may influence the endogenous variables but is never explained by them.↩︎
Estimation is simple in the sense that each equation can be estimated separately by OLS.↩︎
Sims (1980) objected that traditional simultaneous equation models require knowing a priori which variables are exogenous and which regressors belong on the right-hand side of each equation. He regarded such identifying restrictions as incredible, and proposed treating all variables symmetrically as endogenous instead.↩︎
A square matrix is diagonal when every entry off the main diagonal is zero, so only the entries running from top-left to bottom-right can be non-zero. For the covariance matrix \(\Omega = \operatorname{E}[w_t w_t']\), the diagonal entry \(\sigma_i^2 = \operatorname{Var}(w_{it})\) is the variance of equation \(i\)’s error, while the off-diagonal entry \(\sigma_{ij} = \operatorname{Cov}(w_{it}, w_{jt})\) is the covariance between the errors of equations \(i\) and \(j\) at the same date. A diagonal \(\Omega\) would therefore mean every such covariance is zero, that is, the errors of different equations are mutually uncorrelated. Here \(\Omega\) is not diagonal: the off-diagonal entries are generally non-zero, which is precisely the contemporaneous cross-equation correlation left behind by the simultaneity among the variables.↩︎
Two random variables are orthogonal here when their contemporaneous covariance is zero, \(\operatorname{Cov}(w_{it}, w_{jt}) = 0\), since with zero-mean errors this coincides with \(\operatorname{E}[w_{it} w_{jt}] = 0\). Orthogonal residuals would give a diagonal \(\Omega\), each error moving independently of the others. The reduced-form residuals fail this: their off-diagonal covariances are non-zero, so they are not orthogonal. Structural shocks, by contrast, are orthogonal by construction, which is exactly what identification must recover.↩︎
ARDL (AutoRegressive Distributed Lag): a single-equation model in which a dependent variable is explained by its own lags (the autoregressive part) plus current and past values of one or more explanatory variables (the distributed-lag part). For a single regressor:
\[y_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \phi_i\, y_{t-i} + \sum_{j=0}^{q} \beta_j\, x_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t\]↩︎
OLS attributes to a regressor all the co-movement between that regressor and the dependent variable. When the regressor also moves with the error, part of the error’s effect is mistakenly assigned to the regressor: the estimated coefficient \(\hat{\beta}\) absorbs the influence of the error instead of measuring the regressor’s own effect. The estimate is therefore biased, in that its expected value differs from the true parameter, \(\operatorname{E}[\hat{\beta}] \neq \beta\), and inconsistent, in that it does not converge to the true value even as the sample grows without bound.↩︎
Identified VAR: identification means separating correlation from causation. Correlation alone cannot tell us which shock caused what and identification requires assumptions that should be based on economic theory. Remember: The reduced-form residuals are correlated across equations (attention: not inside equations).↩︎
Impulse-response function (IRF): Traces the effect of a one-time shock to one variable on the current and future values of all variables in the system, holding everything else constant. It answers: “if variable X is hit by a shock today, how does variable Y react today, next period, two periods ahead, …?”↩︎
Forecast error variance decomposition (FEVD): At each forecast horizon, splits the forecast error variance of a variable into the share explained by shocks to itself versus shocks to each of the other variables. It answers: “how much of the uncertainty in forecasting X comes from X’s own shocks, and how much from shocks to the other variables?”↩︎

title: 4  From AR to VAR
4  From AR to VAR
text:
The transmission takes a period: In the animation the shock reaches the second variable only one horizon after impact, never at the moment it arrives. There is therefore the implicit assumption that no contemporaneous transmission occurs in either direction. An assumption that is convenient now, to understand how the mechanism works, but almost certainly false, as the previous chapter argued. Restoring the within-period links means restoring the matrix \(B\) that contains the contemporaneous coefficients, here the assumption is basically \(B = I\).
The cross-coefficients are what makes the system a system: Setting both of them to zero splits the model into two univariate AR processes that happen to be plotted on the same axes. A shock to the output gap then stays in the output gap, inflation never moves, and each variable decays at its own rate with nothing passing between them. What the multivariate structure adds is precisely the return channel: the disturbance leaves the equation it hit, comes back one period later altered by the other variable, and the response that results is not something either equation could have produced on its own.
The choice of where the shock hits is itself the problem: The two buttons produce different trajectories, which is unsurprising: an inflation shock is not an output shock. What is worth noticing is what the button actually does. It moves one shock by one unit and holds the other at zero (exactly as if it was a structural shock). In the data that event never occurs, because the reduced-form shocks are correlated: when one moves, the other typically moves with it. The button performs an experiment that the reduced form does not license. It ramains useful here to provide an intuition of what is going to be studied.

title: 4  From AR to VAR
section: 4.2 How to trace the dynamic effect of a shock?
text:
4.2 How to trace the dynamic effect of a shock?
Recursive substitution, dynamic multiplier and Wold representation (infinite moving-average) are usually understood as separate topics. They are not: they are three views of a single question “how does a shock propagate through time?”.
The interactive above already showed the response to a shock, but how is it obtained? The answer comes first in the scalar AR(1) world, where every step is intuitive and easy to understand, and is then replayed in the matrix VAR world, where the algebra is heavier but the logic is identical. The reward is a clean bridge: the moving-average weights, the dynamic multipliers, and the impulse responses are the same object.
3 key definitions:

Recursive substitution: unwinding the model until \(y_t\) is written in terms of past shocks.

Dynamic multiplier: the effect of one shock, horizon by horizon. This is the impulse response.

Wold representation: under the stationarity assumption the influence of the initial value, present in the recursive substitution, fades to zero and only the shock sum survives, this is the infinite moving-average form, whose coefficients are the multipliers of point 2.

title: 4  From AR to VAR
section: 4.4 Part B - The matrix case: VAR(p)
text:
4.4 Part B - The matrix case: VAR(p)
Everything above now repeats with one substitution: scalars become matrices, the logic is the same.

4.4.1 Recursive substitution for the VAR
The reduced-form VAR(1) (again dropping the constant) is the matrix twin of Equation 4.1, with \(Z_t\) stacking the \(n\) variables, \(\Phi\) an \(n\times n\) coefficient matrix, and \(w_t\) the vector of innovations:
\[
Z_t = \Phi\, Z_{t-1} + w_t
\tag{4.22}\]
Substituting, exactly as before, every \(\phi^{\,i}\) becoming \(\Phi^{\,i}\):
\[
Z_t = \Phi^{\,t+1} Z_{-1} + \sum_{i=0}^{t}\Phi^{\,i}\, w_{t-i}
\tag{4.23}\]
Same structure as Equation 4.3: a transient \(\Phi^{\,t+1} Z_{-1}\) plus a weighted sum of past shock vectors, now with matrix weights \(\Phi^{\,i}\).


4.4.2 The VMA(\(\infty\)): the multivariate Wold representation
Letting the process run from the infinite past, if the VAR is stationary the transient dies (\(\Phi^{\,t+1} Z_{-1}\to 0\)) and
\[
Z_t = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\Phi^{\,i}\, w_{t-i}
= \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\Psi_i\, w_{t-i},
\qquad \Psi_i = \Phi^{\,i},\;\; \Psi_0 = I_n
\tag{4.24}\]
This is the VMA(\(\infty\)), the multivariate Wold representation. For a VAR(1) the moving-average matrices are simply the powers \(\Psi_i=\Phi^{\,i}\) the literal analogue of the scalar \(\phi^{\,i}\). For a general VAR(\(p\)) the same object is obtained with the lag operator: writing the model as \(G(L)\,Z_t = w_t\) and inverting the matrix polynomial,
\[
Z_t = \mu + G(L)^{-1} w_t = \mu + \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\Psi_i\, w_{t-i},
\tag{4.25}\]
where the \(\Psi_i\) are the coefficient matrices of the power series \(G(L)^{-1}=\sum_i \Psi_i L^{i}\) (with \(\Psi_0=I_n\)), and \(\mu\) is the mean, restored once the constant is put back.
The parallel with the scalar case is one-to-one:

\(y_t=\phi\, y_{t-1}+w_t\)

\(Z_t=\Phi^{\,t+1}Z_{-1}+\sum_i \Phi^{\,i} w_{t-i}\)

\(\Psi_i\;\;(=\Phi^{\,i}\text{ if }p=1)\)


representation

VMA(\(\infty\))

roots of \(\det G(L)=0\) outside the unit circle

\(\partial y_{t+j}/\partial w_t=\phi^{\,j}\)
\(\partial Z_{t+j}/\partial w_t'=\Psi_j\)





4.4.3 The multiplier becomes the impulse response
Differentiating Equation 4.25 with respect to the shock vector, exactly as in the scalar case:
\[
\frac{\partial\, Z_{t+j}}{\partial\, w_t'} = \Psi_j
\tag{4.26}\]
Each matrix \(\Psi_j\) is the system’s response, \(j\) periods ahead, to a one-unit impulse in the shocks: its \((k,\ell)\) entry is the reaction of variable \(k\) to a shock in variable \(\ell\). Where the scalar multiplier \(\phi^{\,j}\) traced a single decaying (or oscillating, or explosive) path, \(\Psi_j\) now carries both own- and cross-effects, so responses can travel between variables, oscillate, and feed back through the system before dying out — the feedback loop of the previous chapter, made quantitative.
For a bivariate VAR(1) this is a \(2\times2\) grid: each variable’s reaction to each shock. The sliders are the four entries of \(\Phi\); each panel traces an entry of \(\Psi_j=\Phi^{\,j}\) over the horizon \(j\):

viewof phi11 = Inputs.range([-0.95, 0.95], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "Phi 1,1 (x on own lag)"})







viewof phi12 = Inputs.range([-0.95, 0.95], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "Phi 1,2 (x on lagged y)"})







viewof phi21 = Inputs.range([-0.95, 0.95], {value: 0.2, step: 0.05, label: "Phi 2,1 (y on lagged x)"})







viewof phi22 = Inputs.range([-0.95, 0.95], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "Phi 2,2 (y on own lag)"})







{
  const H = 20;
  const Phi = [[phi11, phi12], [phi21, phi22]];
  const mul = (A, B) => [
    [A[0][0]*B[0][0] + A[0][1]*B[1][0], A[0][0]*B[0][1] + A[0][1]*B[1][1]],
    [A[1][0]*B[0][0] + A[1][1]*B[1][0], A[1][0]*B[0][1] + A[1][1]*B[1][1]]
  ];
  const vars = ["x", "y"];
  let Psi = [[1, 0], [0, 1]];
  const rows = [];
  for (let j = 0; j <= H; j++) {
    for (let k = 0; k < 2; k++) {
      for (let l = 0; l < 2; l++) {
        rows.push({
          j,
          resp: Psi[k][l],
          respVar: "response of " + vars[k],
          shockVar: "shock to " + vars[l]
        });
      }
    }
    Psi = mul(Phi, Psi);
  }
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 380,
    marginLeft: 55,
    x: { label: "horizon j" },
    y: { label: "response", grid: true },
    fx: { label: null },
    fy: { label: null },
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
      Plot.barY(rows, {
        x: "j",
        y: "resp",
        fx: "shockVar",
        fy: "respVar",
        fill: d => d.resp >= 0 ? "#4c78a8" : "#e45756"
      })
    ]
  });
}






Try pushing the coefficients up: some combinations put a root of \(\det G(L)\) inside the unit circle and the responses explode instead of dying out — nonstationarity, made visible.


4.4.4 Where this leads
These \(\Psi_j\) are the reduced-form impulse responses: they answer “what happens if the reduced-form innovation \(w_{\ell t}\) moves by one unit?” But the innovations are correlated across equations, so a shock to one variable rarely arrives in isolation — which makes the reduced-form responses hard to read as clean economic experiments. Recovering structural impulse responses, where the shocks are mutually uncorrelated and interpretable, requires identifying the VAR — orthogonalizing the innovations. That is the subject of the next chapter, together with the forecast error variance decomposition, which uses these very same \(\Psi_j\) to split forecast uncertainty across shocks.


4.4.5 From innovations to shocks: the bridge to identification
Up to this point \(w_t\) has been called a shock, loosely. It is time to be precise, because the distinction is what the next chapter is built on.
What Equation 4.22 contains are innovations: a statistical object, defined as the one-step-ahead forecast error — the part of \(Z_t\) that cannot be predicted from its own past,
\[
w_t = Z_t - E\!\left[Z_t \mid Z_{t-1}, Z_{t-2}, \dots\right]
\tag{4.27}\]
that is, the genuinely new information arriving at date \(t\) — hence the name. Nothing in this definition carries economic content: it is a residual, whatever OLS leaves unexplained equation by equation.
A structural shock, by contrast, is an economically meaningful disturbance: a monetary policy shock, a technology shock, a demand shock.
The gap between the two is not a matter of vocabulary, it is a matter of correlation. Reduced-form innovations are correlated across equations:
\[
E\!\left[w_t\, w_t'\right] = \Sigma, \qquad \Sigma \text{ generally non-diagonal}
\tag{4.28}\]
so \(w_{1t}\) is not “the shock to the first variable”: when it moves, the other innovations typically move with it. Asking “what happens if \(w_{1t}\) increases by one unit, holding the others fixed?” describes an event that is never observed in the data — which is why the \(\Psi_j\) of Equation 4.26 are reduced-form impulse responses, correct as a description of the joint dynamics, but not readable as economic experiments.
Recovering structural impulse responses means turning correlated innovations into mutually uncorrelated, interpretable shocks. This is the identification problem: writing \(w_t = B\, u_t\), where the structural shocks \(u_t\) are orthogonal, and finding enough restrictions to pin down \(B\). Two routes are available — a recursive ordering (Cholesky) or restrictions drawn from economic theory — and they are the subject of the next chapter, together with the forecast error variance decomposition, which uses these very same \(\Psi_j\) to split forecast uncertainty across shocks.

The inversion of \((1-\phi L)\) in Equation 4.7 is a geometric series \(\sum_i \phi^{i} L^{i}\) that converges only when \(|\phi| < 1\). If \(|\phi| \ge 1\) the weights do not decay, the sum of past shocks diverges, and no stable MA(\(\infty\)) exists — the process is nonstationary (the random walk \(\phi = 1\) is the borderline case).↩︎
